Reinforcement Learning

Cluster DD.1.2 · Decision Theory and Reinforcement Learning

The Bellman equations and what follows from them: the existence of optimal policies, the policy improvement theorem, the rate of convergence of Bellman updates, and the convergence of Q-learning.

By Leon Lang, David Quarel

  • PDFviewdownload
  • LaTeXdownload
  • Markdowndownload
  • SlidespresenthandoutLaTeX

What you’ll learn
  • Understand Markov Decision Processes and the goal of the agent, for known environments.
  • Understand the Bellman equation.
  • Understand the policy improvement theorem, and how we can use it to iteratively solve for an optimal policy.
  • Prove properties involving the Bellman equations, including the existence of optimal policies, the policy improvement theorem, rate of convergence of Bellman updates, and the convergence of Q-learning.

Setup

In this exercise sheet, we prove a variety of results that are behind the ARENA Intro to RL materials.

An agent interacts with an environment in discrete time steps t=0,1,2,…. On timestep t, the agent observes the current state st​∈S and selects an action at​∈A according to its policy. The environment then responds with a reward rt+1​∈R and a new state st+1​∈S. (The reward and next state are indexed by t+1 because they are produced by the environment after the agent's action.) The goal is to act so as to maximize expected discounted future reward.

These environments are called Markov decision processes (MDPs). They satisfy two key properties: (i) stationarity — the transition and reward functions do not change over time, and (ii) the Markov property — the distribution over the next state and reward depends only on the current state and action, not on the full history of past interactions. Together, these properties mean that the current state st​ is a sufficient summary of the past for the purpose of choosing optimal actions.

Definition 0.1 (Spaces and notation). - S — finite state space

  • A — finite action space
  • γ∈(0,1) — discount factor
  • ΔX — set of all probability distributions over a set X
  • [[P]] — Iverson bracket: 1 if P is true, 0 if false

Definition 0.2 (Environment). An MDP environment is specified by a pair (T,R):

  • T:S×A→ΔS is the transition kernel: given state s and action a, the next state is drawn s′∼T(⋅∣s,a).
  • R:S×A×S→R is the reward function: on a transition from s to s′ under action a, the agent receives reward R(s,a,s′). 1

Definition 0.3 (Policy). A policy π:S→ΔA maps each state to a probability distribution over actions. Given state s:

  • π(⋅∣s) is a distribution over A,
  • π(a∣s)∈[0,1] is the probability of choosing action a,
  • the agent samples a∼π(⋅∣s).

A policy is deterministic if π(a∣s)∈{0,1} for all a,s. In this case, we abuse notation and write π(s):=argmaxa∈A​π(a∣s) for the unique action selected at state s.

Definition 0.4 (Trajectory). When policy π interacts with environment (T,R) starting from initial state s0​, the resulting trajectory (s0​,a0​,r1​,s1​,a1​,r2​,s2​,a2​,r3​,…) is generated by

ak​∼π(⋅∣sk​),sk+1​∼T(⋅∣sk​,ak​),rk+1​=R(sk​,ak​,sk+1​),

for k=0,1,2,…. We write Eπ​[⋅] for expectations over such trajectories.

1. The Bellman equation

Definition 1.1 (Return). The return from time t is the discounted sum of future rewards:

Gt​:=k=t+1∑∞​γk−t−1rk​=rt+1​+γrt+2​+γ2rt+3​+⋯.

It satisfies the recursion

Gt​=rt+1​+γGt+1​.

Definition 1.2 (Value function). The value function of a policy π is the expected return when starting from state s and acting according to π:

​Vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s]=Eπ​[rt+1​+γrt+2​+γ2rt+3​+⋯​st​=s]=at​∈A∑​π(at​∣s)st+1​∈S∑​T(st+1​∣s,at​)at+1​∈A∑​π(at+1​∣st+1​)st+2​∈S∑​T(st+2​∣st+1​,at+1​)⋯[R(s,at​,st+1​)+γR(st+1​,at+1​,st+2​)+γ2R(st+2​,at+2​,st+3​)+⋯].​

The expectation averages the return over all future trajectories (at​,st+1​,at+1​,st+2​,…) generated by sampling ak​∼π(⋅∣sk​) and sk+1​∼T(⋅∣sk​,ak​), starting from st​=s.

Exercise 1.1. Prove the Bellman equation: for all s∈S,

Bellman Equation

Vπ​(s)=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′)).

Hint: condition on the first action and the first transition, then separate the immediate reward from the remaining return.

Solution

Starting from the definition of Vπ​ and using the recursion Gt​=rt+1​+γGt+1​:

Vπ​(s)​=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s]=Eπ​[rt+1​+γGt+1​∣st​=s].​

Now condition on the first action at​=a and the first transition st+1​=s′:

Vπ​(s)​=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)×Eπ​[rt+1​+γGt+1​∣st​=s,at​=a,st+1​=s′].​

Given st​=s, at​=a, and st+1​=s′, the immediate reward is deterministic: rt+1​=R(s,a,s′). For the remaining return, by the Markov property the future trajectory from time t+1 onward depends only on st+1​=s′, so

Eπ​[Gt+1​∣st​=s,at​=a,st+1​=s′]=Eπ​[Gt+1​∣st+1​=s′]=Vπ​(s′).

Substituting both back gives

Vπ​(s)=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′)).

Definition 1.3 (Action-value function). The action-value function (or Q-function) of π is the expected return starting from state s, taking action a, and acting according to π thereafter:

Qπ​(s,a)=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s,at​=a].

Exercise 1.2. (a) Express Vπ​(s) in terms of Qπ​.

(b) Express Qπ​(s,a) in terms of Vπ​.

(c) Using these relations, derive a recursive equation for Qπ​ analogous to the Bellman equation above.

Solution

(a) Starting from the definition of Vπ​(s) and conditioning on the first action at​=a:

Vπ​(s)​=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s]=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s,at​=a]=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)Qπ​(s,a).​

(b) Starting from the definition of Qπ​(s,a) and using the recursion Gt​=rt+1​+γGt+1​, we condition on the first transition st+1​=s′:

Qπ​(s,a)​=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s,at​=a]=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)Eπ​[rt+1​+γGt+1​∣st​=s,at​=a,st+1​=s′]=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′)),​

where the last step uses rt+1​=R(s,a,s′) (deterministic given st​,at​,st+1​) and the Markov property Eπ​[Gt+1​∣st+1​=s′]=Vπ​(s′).

(c) Substituting Exercise 1.2(a) into Exercise 1.2(b), replacing Vπ​(s′) by its expression in terms of Qπ​:

Qπ​(s,a)=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γa′∈A∑​π(a′∣s′)Qπ​(s′,a′)).

This is the Bellman equation for the action-value function. Note also that substituting Exercise 1.2(b) into Exercise 1.2(a) recovers the Bellman equation for Vπ​ from Exercise 1.1.

2. An example MDP

Consider the MDP with state space S={s0​,sL​,sR​}, action space A={aL​,aR​}, and deterministic transitions as shown:

From s0​, action aL​ leads deterministically to sL​ with reward +1, and action aR​ leads deterministically to sR​ with reward +0. From sL​ (resp. sR​), any action returns to s0​ with reward +0 (resp. +2).

Let πL​ denote the policy that always selects aL​, and πR​ the policy that always selects aR​.

Exercise 2.1. Using the Bellman equation from Exercise 1.1, verify that

VπL​​(s0​)=1−γ21​,VπR​​(s0​)=1−γ22γ​.
Solution

Under πL​ all transitions are deterministic, so the Bellman equation collapses to

VπL​​(s0​)VπL​​(sL​)​=R(s0​,aL​,sL​)+γVπL​​(sL​)=1+γVπL​​(sL​),=R(sL​,aL​,s0​)+γVπL​​(s0​)=0+γVπL​​(s0​).​

Substituting the second into the first gives VπL​​(s0​)=1+γ2VπL​​(s0​), hence

VπL​​(s0​)=1−γ21​.

Similarly, under πR​:

VπR​​(s0​)VπR​​(sR​)​=R(s0​,aR​,sR​)+γVπR​​(sR​)=0+γVπR​​(sR​),=R(sR​,aR​,s0​)+γVπR​​(s0​)=2+γVπR​​(s0​).​

Substituting yields VπR​​(s0​)=γ(2+γVπR​​(s0​))=2γ+γ2VπR​​(s0​), hence

VπR​​(s0​)=1−γ22γ​.

Exercise 2.2. Determine the best action from state s0​ as a function of the discount factor γ∈(0,1). Show that the breakeven point is γ=21​.

Solution

Since any action from sL​ or sR​ deterministically returns to s0​ with the same reward, the value of any policy at s0​ is determined entirely by the action chosen at s0​. Hence comparing VπL​​(s0​) and VπR​​(s0​) suffices:

VπL​​(s0​)−VπR​​(s0​)=1−γ21−2γ​.

Since 1−γ2>0 for γ∈(0,1), the sign is determined by 1−2γ:

  • γ<21​: aL​ is optimal — the immediate reward of 1 outweighs a discounted future reward of 2.
  • γ>21​: aR​ is optimal — the agent is patient enough to wait one step for the larger reward.
  • γ=21​: both actions are equally good (breakeven), and each gives V∗(s0​)=34​.

3. Bellman operators and the existence of optimal policies

Banach fixed-point theorem

In this and the following exercises, we will make use of the well-known Banach fixed point theorem:

Theorem 3.1 (Banach Fixed Point Theorem). Let (X,d) be a complete metric space and let F:X→X be a contraction mapping, i.e. there exists γ∈[0,1) such that

d(F(x),F(y))≤γd(x,y)for all x,y∈X.

Then F has a unique fixed point x∗∈X satisfying F(x∗)=x∗. Moreover, for any initial point x0​∈X, one

has limn→∞​d(Fn(x0​),x∗)=0 where Fn is the n-fold composition of F with itself. That is, Fn(x0​) converges to x∗ with respect to the metric d.

The problem

Definition 3.2 (Bellman optimality operator). Let V={V:S→R} denote the vector space of value functions, equipped with the sup-norm ∥V∥∞​=maxs∈S​∣V(s)∣. The Bellman optimality operator B:V→V is defined by

(BV)(s):=a∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γV(s′)).

Exercise 3.1. Let f,g:A→R be real-valued functions on a finite set A. Prove that

​a∈Amax​f(a)−a∈Amax​g(a)​≤a∈Amax​∣f(a)−g(a)∣.
Solution

Without loss of generality, assume maxa​f(a)≥maxa​g(a). Let a∗∈argmaxa∈A​f(a). Then:

​a∈Amax​f(a)−a∈Amax​g(a)​​=a∈Amax​f(a)−a∈Amax​g(a)=f(a∗)−a∈Amax​g(a)≤f(a∗)−g(a∗)=∣f(a∗)−g(a∗)∣≤a∈Amax​∣f(a)−g(a)∣.​

Exercise 3.2. Using Exercise 3.1, prove that B is a contraction mapping with contraction factor γ, i.e. for all V,W∈V,

∥BV−BW∥∞​≤γ∥V−W∥∞​.
Solution

Fix an arbitrary state s∈S. Define for each a∈A:

f(a)g(a)​:=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γV(s′)),:=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γW(s′)).​

Then (BV)(s)=maxa​f(a) and (BW)(s)=maxa​g(a). By Exercise 3.1:

​(BV)(s)−(BW)(s)​​≤a∈Amax​​f(a)−g(a)​=a∈Amax​​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)γ(V(s′)−W(s′))​≤γa∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)​V(s′)−W(s′)​≤γa∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)∥V−W∥∞​≤γ∥V−W∥∞​,​

where the last step uses ∑s′​T(s′∣s,a)=1. Since this holds for every s∈S, taking the maximum over s gives ∥BV−BW∥∞​≤γ∥V−W∥∞​.

Exercise 3.3. Using Theorem 3.1, conclude that there exists a unique V∗∈V satisfying BV∗=V∗, and that for any initial V0​∈V, the iterates BnV0​→V∗ as n→∞.

Solution

The space (V,∥⋅∥∞​) is a finite-dimensional normed vector space, hence complete. By Exercise 3.2, B is a contraction on V with factor γ<1. Theorem 3.1 then gives the existence of a unique fixed point V∗=BV∗, and convergence BnV0​→V∗ for any V0​∈V.

Exercise 3.4. Show that for any policy π, the operator Bπ​:V→V defined by

Bellman Policy Operator

(Bπ​V)(s):=a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γV(s′))

is also a contraction with factor γ. Conclude that Vπ​ is its unique fixed point and that Bπn​V0​→Vπ​ for any initial V0​∈V as n→∞.

Remark. This shows that the numerical policy evaluation algorithm from the ARENA materials converges to the correct solution.

Solution

Fix V,W∈V and an arbitrary state s∈S. Then:

​(Bπ​V)(s)−(Bπ​W)(s)​​=​a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)γ(V(s′)−W(s′))​≤γa∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)​V(s′)−W(s′)​≤γa∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)∥V−W∥∞​≤γ∥V−W∥∞​,​

where the last step uses ∑s′​T(s′∣s,a)=1 and ∑a​π(a∣s)=1. Taking the maximum over s gives ∥Bπ​V−Bπ​W∥∞​≤γ∥V−W∥∞​, so Bπ​ is a contraction with factor γ.

By Theorem 3.1, Bπ​ has a unique fixed point. By the Bellman equation (Section 1), Vπ​ satisfies Bπ​Vπ​=Vπ​, so Vπ​ is this unique fixed point. The convergence statement also follows from Theorem 3.1.

Exercise 3.5. Let V∈V be any value function, and let πV​ be a greedy policy with respect to V, i.e.

πV​(s)∈a∈Aargmax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γV(s′)).

Show that BπV​​V=BV.

Solution

Since πV​ is deterministic, πV​(a∣s)=[[a=πV​(s)]], so the sum over a in BπV​​ collapses to the single term a=πV​(s). For every s∈S:

(BπV​​V)(s)​=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,πV​(s))(R(s,πV​(s),s′)+γV(s′))=a∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γV(s′))=(BV)(s),​

where the second equality holds because πV​(s) selects a maximizing action by definition.

Exercise 3.6. Define the greedy policy with respect to V∗ by π∗=πV∗​ as in the previous part. Show that Vπ∗​=V∗, i.e. the value function of π∗ equals the fixed point of B.

Hint: show that V∗ satisfies the same fixed-point equation as Vπ∗​.

Solution

We have Bπ∗​V∗=BV∗=V∗ by Exercise 3.5 and Exercise 3.3. So V∗ is a fixed point of Bπ∗​. By Exercise 3.4, Vπ∗​ is the unique fixed point of Bπ∗​. Therefore Vπ∗​=V∗.

Exercise 3.7. Conclude that π∗ is an optimal policy: for every policy π and every state s∈S,

Vπ∗​(s)≥Vπ​(s).

Hint: show that BVπ​≥Vπ​ pointwise, then iterate and take the limit.

Solution

Let π be any policy. Since the max over actions is at least as large as any weighted average:

(BV)(s)≥(Bπ​V)(s)for all V∈V,s∈S.

In particular, since Vπ​ is a fixed point of Bπ​ (Exercise 3.4):

(BVπ​)(s)≥(Bπ​Vπ​)(s)=Vπ​(s)for all s∈S.

Note that B is monotone: if V(s)≥W(s) for all s, then (BV)(s)≥(BW)(s). Applying B to both sides and using monotonicity, then iterating:

Vπ​≤BVπ​≤B2Vπ​≤⋯≤BnVπ​.

By Exercise 3.3, BnVπ​→V∗ as n→∞. Taking the limit:

Vπ​(s)≤V∗(s)=Vπ∗​(s)for all s∈S,

where the last equality is Exercise 3.6. Since π was arbitrary, π∗ is optimal.

4. Policy improvement theorem

Given a policy π, define the improved policy π′ greedily with respect to Vπ​:

Policy Improvement

π′(s)∈a∈Aargmax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′)).

Exercise 4.1. In proving Exercise 3.7, we already saw that for all s∈S, we have (BVπ​)(s)≥Vπ​(s). When does equality hold for all states?

Solution

We have

(BVπ​)(s)​=a∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′))≥a∈A∑​π(a∣s)s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)(R(s,a,s′)+γVπ​(s′))=Vπ​(s),​

where we used the Bellman equation in the last step. If equality holds at every state s, then Vπ​ is a fixed point of B, which by uniqueness (Exercise 3.3) means Vπ​=V∗=Vπ∗​, i.e. π is already optimal by Exercise 3.7.

Exercise 4.2. Show that Vπ′​(s)≥Vπ​(s) for all s∈S.

Hint: show that Bπ′​Vπ​≥Vπ​ pointwise using Exercise 3.5, then iterate Bπ′​ and take the limit.

Solution

By Exercise 3.5, Bπ′​Vπ​=BVπ​≥Vπ​ pointwise, where the inequality is from Exercise 4.1. Note that Bπ′​ is monotone: if V(s)≥W(s) for all s, then (Bπ′​V)(s)≥(Bπ′​W)(s). Applying Bπ′​ to both sides and iterating:

Vπ​≤Bπ′​Vπ​≤Bπ′2​Vπ​≤⋯≤Bπ′n​Vπ​.

By Exercise 3.4, Bπ′n​Vπ​→Vπ′​ as n→∞. Taking the limit gives Vπ′​(s)≥Vπ​(s) for all s∈S.

Exercise 4.3. The policy iteration algorithm generates a sequence of policies π0​,π1​,π2​,… where each πk+1​ is the greedy policy with respect to Vπk​​. Show that this sequence converges to an optimal policy π∗ in a finite number of steps.

Hint: how many deterministic policies are there?

Solution

By Exercise 4.2, the sequence of value functions is monotonically improving: Vπk+1​​(s)≥Vπk​​(s) for all s and all k. Since each πk​ is a deterministic policy and there are only ∣A∣∣S∣ deterministic policies, the sequence must eventually revisit a policy. If πk+1​=πj​ for some j≤k, then Vπk+1​​=Vπj​​, and by monotonicity Vπj​​=Vπj+1​​=⋯=Vπk+1​​. In particular Vπk​​=Vπk+1​​.

It remains to show this implies optimality. Since πk+1​ is greedy with respect to Vπk​​, Exercise 3.5 gives BVπk​​=Bπk+1​​Vπk​​. Since Vπk+1​​ is the fixed point of Bπk+1​​ and Vπk​​=Vπk+1​​, we get Bπk+1​​Vπk​​=Vπk​​. Combining: BVπk​​=Vπk​​, so πk​ is optimal by Exercise 4.1.

5. Bellman convergence rate

Exercise 3.3 showed that the iterates Vn​:=BnV0​ converge to V∗ for any starting V0​∈V, but it did not tell us how fast, nor how to decide when to stop iterating. We derive some convergence rate bounds (Puterman 1994, Chapter 6).

Exercise 5.1. Show that for any initial V0​∈V, the iterates Vn​:=BnV0​ satisfy

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤γn∥V0​−V∗∥∞​.

Remark. This bound is not useful as a stopping criterion in practice as it depends on the unknown V∗.

Solution

Since V∗=BV∗ and B is a γ-contraction (Exercise 3.2),

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​=∥BVn−1​−BV∗∥∞​≤γ∥Vn−1​−V∗∥∞​.

Iterating n times gives ∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤γn∥V0​−V∗∥∞​.

Exercise 5.2. Show the a priori bound:

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.

This bound uses only ∥V1​−V0​∥∞​ — a quantity computable after a single iteration, independent of V∗.

Hint: write V∗−Vn​=∑k=n∞​(Vk+1​−Vk​) (valid since Vk​→V∗), and bound each term using the contraction of B.

Solution

By the contraction property applied repeatedly,

∥Vk+1​−Vk​∥∞​​=∥BVk​−BVk−1​∥∞​≤γ∥Vk​−Vk−1​∥∞​≤⋯≤γk∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.​

Since Vk​→V∗ (Exercise 3.3), we have the telescoping identity V∗−Vn​=∑k=n∞​(Vk+1​−Vk​). Applying the triangle inequality and the geometric bound above:

∥V∗−Vn​∥∞​​≤k=n∑∞​∥Vk+1​−Vk​∥∞​≤k=n∑∞​γk∥V1​−V0​∥∞​=1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.​

Exercise 5.3. Show the a posteriori bound: for n≥1,

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤1−γγ​∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​.

Hint: telescope from n as in Exercise 5.2, but bound ∥Vk+1​−Vk​∥∞​ in terms of ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​ instead.

Solution

Step 1: bound each successive difference in terms of ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​. Apply the contraction property of B once:

∥Vn+1​−Vn​∥∞​=∥BVn​−BVn−1​∥∞​≤γ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​.

Apply it again, chaining with the previous bound:

∥Vn+2​−Vn+1​∥∞​≤γ∥Vn+1​−Vn​∥∞​≤γ2∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​.

Continuing this pattern, for every j≥0:

∥Vn+j+1​−Vn+j​∥∞​≤γj+1∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​.

Step 2: telescope. Since Vk​→V∗ (Exercise 3.3), we have the telescoping identity

V∗−Vn​=(Vn+1​−Vn​)+(Vn+2​−Vn+1​)+(Vn+3​−Vn+2​)+⋯.

Applying the triangle inequality and the bounds from Step 1:

∥V∗−Vn​∥∞​​≤∥Vn+1​−Vn​∥∞​+∥Vn+2​−Vn+1​∥∞​+∥Vn+3​−Vn+2​∥∞​+⋯≤γ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​+γ2∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​+γ3∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​+⋯=(γ+γ2+γ3+⋯)∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​=1−γγ​∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​.​

Exercise 5.4. Show that the a posteriori bound of Exercise 5.3 is always at least as tight as the a priori bound of Exercise 5.2: for all n≥1,

1−γγ​∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​≤1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.

Hint: bound ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​ by repeated application of the contraction.

Solution

Apply the contraction property of B to Vn​=BVn−1​ and Vn−1​=BVn−2​:

∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​≤γ∥Vn−1​−Vn−2​∥∞​.

Continuing this n−1 times altogether, we eventually land on ∥V1​−V0​∥∞​:

∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​≤γn−1∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.

Multiplying both sides by 1−γγ​>0 preserves the inequality:

1−γγ​∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​≤1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​.

Both bounds from Exercise 5.3 and Exercise 5.2 upper-bound ∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​, and the a posteriori one is smaller.

Exercise 5.5. Assume ∣R(s,a,s′)∣≤Rmax​ for all s,a,s′. Show that if we initialize with V0​≡0, then

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤1−γγn​Rmax​.

This bound depends only on n, γ, and Rmax​, so it can be evaluated before running a single iteration.

Solution

With V0​≡0:

V1​(s)=(BV0​)(s)=a∈Amax​s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)R(s,a,s′).

Each term is a convex combination of rewards, all bounded in absolute value by Rmax​, so ∣V1​(s)∣≤Rmax​ for every s, hence ∥V1​−V0​∥∞​=∥V1​∥∞​≤Rmax​. Substituting into the a priori bound of Exercise 5.2:

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​≤1−γγn​Rmax​.

Exercise 5.6. Show that the bound of Exercise 5.5 is tight: exhibit an MDP in which ∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​=1−γγn​Rmax​ for every n≥0 (with V0​≡0).

Solution

Take S={s}, A={a}, T(s∣s,a)=1, and R(s,a,s)=Rmax​. The Bellman optimality operator collapses to

(BV)(s)=Rmax​+γV(s).

Starting from V0​(s)=0 and iterating,

Vn​(s)=Rmax​(1+γ+γ2+⋯+γn−1)=Rmax​⋅1−γ1−γn​.

The fixed point V∗(s) solves V∗(s)=Rmax​+γV∗(s), giving V∗(s)=Rmax​/(1−γ). Therefore

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​=V∗(s)−Vn​(s)=1−γRmax​​−1−γRmax​(1−γn)​=1−γγn​Rmax​,

so the bound of Exercise 5.5 is attained with equality. No bound in terms of only n, γ, and Rmax​ can be sharper.

Remark. Combining Exercise 5.3, 5.2 and 5.5 gives a chain of progressively weaker but increasingly upfront-computable bounds:

Convergence Bounds

∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​​≤a posteriori, tightest1−γγ​∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​​​≤a priori1−γγn​∥V1​−V0​∥∞​​​≤upfront, assumes V0​≡0,∣R∣≤Rmax​1−γγn​Rmax​​​.​

Each step weakens the bound by replacing realized information with something coarser: first the most recent step size ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​ with the worst-case geometric decay γn−1∥V1​−V0​∥∞​ (contraction of B applied n−1 times), then the initial step size ∥V1​−V0​∥∞​ with the crude reward bound Rmax​. In practice the leftmost bound is significantly tighter, since ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​ often decays strictly faster than γn−1∥V1​−V0​∥∞​. It also yields a concrete stopping rule: to guarantee ∥Vn​−V∗∥∞​≤ε, iterate until ∥Vn​−Vn−1​∥∞​≤γ1−γ​ε.

6. Convergence of Q-learning

The policy improvement theorem from Section 4 shows that we can in principle find an optimal policy in MDPs. However, it makes the uncomfortable assumption that we know the environment dynamics via the transition kernel T. In this problem, we prove that Q-learning, which does not make such an assumption, converges to the optimal action-value function, from which one can trivially extract an optimal policy by choosing actions greedily.

Stochastic approximation theorem

We will make use of the following stochastic approximation result, which we state without proof:

Theorem 6.1 (Stochastic Approximation for Contractions (Tsitsiklis 1994, Theorem 3)). Let X={x:I→R} be the space of real-valued functions on a finite set I, equipped with the sup-norm ∥x∥∞​=maxi​∣x(i)∣. Let F:X→X be a contraction mapping with factor γ∈[0,1) and unique fixed point x∗.

Fix an initial iterate x0​∈X, and for each t≥0 let αt​:I→[0,1] be a learning rate function and wt​:I→R a random noise function (both functions on I, one value per coordinate). Consider the stochastic iteration

xt+1​(i)=(1−αt​(i))xt​(i)+αt​(i)[F(xt​)(i)+wt​(i)]for all i∈I,

where updates are applied to a single coordinate i=it​ at each step (i.e. αt​(i)=0 for i=it​). Suppose:

(a) (Learning rate) For each i∈I:

t=0∑∞​αt​(i)=∞,t=0∑∞​αt​(i)2<∞,αt​(i)∈[0,1].

(b) (Noise) For each i∈I, conditioned on the history Ft​={x0​,α0​,w0​,α1​,w1​,…,αt−1​,wt−1​,xt​,αt​}, the noise has zero mean and bounded variance:

E[wt​(i)∣Ft​]=0,E[wt​(i)2∣Ft​]≤C(1+∥xt​∥∞2​)

for some constant C>0.

Then xt​(i)→x∗(i) for all i∈I, with probability 1.

What is stochastic? The randomness of the iteration is carried by the noise: each wt​(i) is a real-valued random variable, and wt​ is a random element of RI. Consequently, the iterates x1​,x2​,… are random (they depend on past noise w0​,…,wt−1​), and the learning rates αt​(i) may be random as well if they depend on the history—e.g. on which coordinate was just visited. The contraction F, its fixed point x∗, the update rule itself, and the initial iterate x0​ are all deterministic. The theorem asserts that despite the noise, the random sequence (xt​) converges pointwise to x∗ almost surely.

Remark on "with probability 1". The conclusion xt​(i)→x∗(i) with probability 1 (also called almost sure convergence) means

P(t→∞lim​xt​(i)=x∗(i))=1for all i∈I.

In other words, the probability that a run of the stochastic iteration fails to converge to x∗ is zero.

Why should we believe this? It helps to build up the result in three layers of increasing complexity.

Layer 1: no noise, all coordinates at once. If wt​=0 and αt​(i)=1 for all i and t, the iteration reduces to xt+1​=F(xt​). This converges to x∗ by Theorem 3.1.

Layer 2: noise, but all coordinates at once. Now suppose we observe F(xt​)+wt​ instead of F(xt​), and use a decreasing step size:

xt+1​=(1−αt​)xt​+αt​[F(xt​)+wt​]=xt​+αt​[signalF(xt​)−xt​​​+noisewt​​​].

The signal F(xt​)−xt​ always points toward x∗ (this is what the contraction property buys us). The noise wt​ is mean-zero, so it pushes us in random directions that partially cancel over time. The two conditions on the step size mediate between signal and noise:

  • ∑αt​=∞ ensures the total step size is large enough to reach x∗ from any starting point.
  • ∑αt2​<∞ ensures the noise averages out. Each noise term wt​ enters the iteration scaled by αt​, contributing a random displacement of size αt​wt​. Although these displacements are not independent (each depends on the current iterate xt​), they are mean-zero conditioned on the past. For such sequences, the variance of the cumulative sum is the sum of the individual variances, which is proportional to ∑αt2​. Since this is finite, the total random drift converges and cannot overwhelm the steady pull of the signal toward x∗.

The signal accumulates coherently (always pulling toward x∗), while the noise averages out.

Layer 3: one coordinate at a time. The iteration updates only one coordinate i=it​ per step, while the others stay frozen. This makes the analysis more difficult since the target F(xt​)(i) depends on all coordinates, including stale ones. The condition ∑t​αt​(i)=∞ for each i ensures no coordinate is permanently neglected, and the contraction property of F provides enough global coupling to prevent coordinates from drifting apart. Making this rigorous is the main technical content of the proof.

The problem

Consider the following generalization of the Q-learning update from the ARENA materials, now with a time-varying learning rate αt​>0: given a current estimate Qt​:S×A→R and an observed transition (st​,at​,rt+1​,st+1​) where st+1​∼T(⋅∣st​,at​) and rt+1​=R(st​,at​,st+1​), the update is

Q-Learning Update

Qt+1​(st​,at​)=Qt​(st​,at​)+αt​(rt+1​+γa′∈Amax​Qt​(st+1​,a′)−Qt​(st​,at​)),

with Qt+1​(s,a)=Qt​(s,a) for all (s,a)=(st​,at​). We will show that, under appropriate conditions, Q-learning converges to the optimal action-value function Q∗.

Let Q={Q:S×A→R} denote the space of action-value functions, equipped with the sup-norm ∥Q∥∞​=maxs,a​∣Q(s,a)∣.

Exercise 6.1. Overloading the notation from Definition 3.2, define the Bellman optimality operator on action-value functions, B:Q→Q, by

Bellman Q-Operator

(BQ)(s,a):=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)[R(s,a,s′)+γa′∈Amax​Q(s′,a′)].

(Here B takes a Q-function to a Q-function, whereas the earlier B in Definition 3.2 takes a V-function to a V-function — whether B denotes the V- or Q-version is always clear from its argument.) Show that B is a γ-contraction on (Q,∥⋅∥∞​).

Hint: this is similar to the proof of Exercise 3.2.

Solution

Fix Q,Q′∈Q and (s,a)∈S×A. By the inequality from Exercise 3.1 (applied at each s′) and the triangle inequality:

​​(BQ)(s,a)−(BQ′)(s,a)​=​s′∑​T(s′∣s,a)γ(a′max​Q(s′,a′)−a′max​Q′(s′,a′))​≤s′∑​T(s′∣s,a)γa′max​​Q(s′,a′)−Q′(s′,a′)​≤s′∑​T(s′∣s,a)γa′,s′′max​​Q(s′′,a′)−Q′(s′′,a′)​≤γ∥Q−Q′∥∞​.​

Taking the maximum over (s,a) gives ∥BQ−BQ′∥∞​≤γ∥Q−Q′∥∞​.

Exercise 6.2. Define Q∗:=Qπ∗​, the action-value function of the optimal policy π∗ from Section 3. We now show Bellman optimality equations and their consequences.

(a) Show that Q∗(s,a)=∑s′∈S​T(s′∣s,a)[R(s,a,s′)+γV∗(s′)].

(b) Show that V∗(s)=maxa∈A​Q∗(s,a).

(c) Conclude that Q∗ is the unique fixed point of B.

Solution

(a) By Exercise 1.2(b) applied to π∗:

Qπ∗​(s,a)=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,a)[R(s,a,s′)+γVπ∗​(s′)].

By Exercise 3.6, Vπ∗​=V∗. Substituting gives the result.

(b) By Exercise 1.2(a), Vπ∗​(s)=∑a​π∗(a∣s)Qπ∗​(s,a). Since π∗ is the greedy policy with respect to V∗ (Exercise 3.5 and 3.6), it is deterministic and selects π∗(s)∈argmaxa​∑s′​T(s′∣s,a)[R(s,a,s′)+γV∗(s′)]. By Exercise 6.2(a), the inner expression equals Q∗(s,a), so π∗(s)∈argmaxa​Q∗(s,a). Since π∗ is deterministic, V∗(s)=Vπ∗​(s)=Qπ∗​(s,π∗(s))=Q∗(s,π∗(s))=maxa​Q∗(s,a).

(c) Substituting Exercise 6.2(b) into Exercise 6.2(a):

Q∗(s,a)=s′∑​T(s′∣s,a)[R(s,a,s′)+γa′max​Q∗(s′,a′)]=(BQ∗)(s,a).

So Q∗ is a fixed point of B. Uniqueness follows from Exercise 6.1 and Theorem 3.1.

Exercise 6.3. Rewrite the Q-learning update in the form of Theorem 6.1:

xt+1​(i)=(1−αt​(i))xt​(i)+αt​(i)[F(xt​)(i)+wt​(i)].

Specifically, identify the index set I, the mapping F, the iterates xt​, and the learning rates αt​(i). Then give an explicit expression for the noise wt​.

Solution

The identifications are:

  • Index set: I=S×A.
  • Iterates: xt​=Qt​.
  • Contraction: F=B, with fixed point x∗=Q∗ (Exercise 6.2).
  • Learning rates: αt​(s,a)=αt​⋅[[(s,a)=(st​,at​)]].

With these identifications, the Q-learning update becomes

Qt+1​(s,a)=(1−αt​(s,a))Qt​(s,a)+αt​(s,a)[(BQt​)(s,a)+wt​(s,a)],

where the noise at the updated coordinate is

wt​(st​,at​)=R(st​,at​,st+1​)+γa′max​Qt​(st+1​,a′)−(BQt​)(st​,at​),

i.e. the difference between the sampled target (using the single transition st+1​) and its expectation over all possible transitions. For (s,a)=(st​,at​), we set wt​(s,a)=0.

Exercise 6.4. Show that the noise satisfies E[wt​(s,a)∣Ft​]=0 for all (s,a)∈S×A, where Ft​ denotes the history up to time t as in Theorem 6.1.

Hint: conditioned on Ft​, the quantities Qt​, st​, and at​ are all determined. What is the only remaining source of randomness?

Solution

Conditioned on Ft​, the quantities Qt​, st​, at​ are all determined. The only remaining randomness is in st+1​∼T(⋅∣st​,at​). Therefore:

​E[wt​(st​,at​)∣Ft​]=E[R(st​,at​,st+1​)+γa′max​Qt​(st+1​,a′)∣Ft​]−(BQt​)(st​,at​)=s′∑​T(s′∣st​,at​)[R(st​,at​,s′)+γa′max​Qt​(s′,a′)]−(BQt​)(st​,at​)=(BQt​)(st​,at​)−(BQt​)(st​,at​)=0.​

For (s,a)=(st​,at​), we have wt​(s,a)=0 by definition, so E[wt​(s,a)∣Ft​]=0 trivially.

Exercise 6.5. Assume ∣R(s,a,s′)∣≤Rmax​ for all s,a,s′. Show that there exists a constant C>0 (depending only on Rmax​ and γ) such that

E[wt​(s,a)2∣Ft​]≤C(1+∥Qt​∥∞2​).

Hint: first show that ∣wt​(st​,at​)∣≤2(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​).

Solution

Step 1: a pointwise bound on wt​. Using ∣R(st​,at​,st+1​)∣≤Rmax​ and ∣maxa′​Qt​(st+1​,a′)∣≤∥Qt​∥∞​, the sampled target satisfies

​R(st​,at​,st+1​)+γa′max​Qt​(st+1​,a′)​≤Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​.

The same bound holds for ∣(BQt​)(st​,at​)∣, since it is a convex combination (over s′) of terms each bounded by Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​. By the triangle inequality:

∣wt​(st​,at​)∣≤2(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​).

This bound holds for every realization of st+1​, not just in expectation.

Step 2: passing to the conditional second moment. Squaring the pointwise bound,

wt​(st​,at​)2≤4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2a.s.

Taking conditional expectation of both sides given Ft​ preserves the inequality (monotonicity of conditional expectation):

E[wt​(st​,at​)2∣Ft​]≤E[4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2∣Ft​].

Now we simplify the right-hand side. It is a function of Qt​ (and the constants Rmax​,γ), and Qt​ is determined once we condition on Ft​ (recall Ft​ records Q0​,Q1​,…,Qt​). So the right-hand side is Ft​-measurable: given the history, it is a fixed real number, not random. Conditional expectation acts as the identity on Ft​-measurable quantities — i.e. E[Y∣Ft​]=Y when Y is Ft​-measurable — so

E[4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2∣Ft​]=4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2.

Combining,

E[wt​(st​,at​)2∣Ft​]≤4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2.

Step 3: putting it in the required form. We want a constant C such that the right-hand side is bounded by C(1+∥Qt​∥∞2​). Applying (a+b)2≤2(a2+b2) with a=Rmax​, b=γ∥Qt​∥∞​:

4(Rmax​+γ∥Qt​∥∞​)2​≤8(Rmax2​+γ2∥Qt​∥∞2​)≤8max(Rmax2​,γ2)(1+∥Qt​∥∞2​).​

So C=8max(Rmax2​,γ2) works. For (s,a)=(st​,at​), we have wt​(s,a)=0, so the bound holds trivially with the same C.

Exercise 6.6. Conclude: state the conditions on the learning rate schedule and the exploration policy under which Q-learning converges, i.e. Qt​→Q∗ with probability 1. Remark. The ARENA implementation uses a constant learning rate α, which does not satisfy ∑t​αt​(s,a)2<∞. In practice, constant-rate Q-learning does not converge exactly but oscillates in a neighbourhood of Q∗ whose size shrinks with α.

Solution

By Exercises 6.1–6.5, the Q-learning iteration satisfies all the hypotheses of Theorem 6.1, provided the learning rate conditions hold: for each (s,a)∈S×A,

t=0∑∞​αt​(s,a)=∞,t=0∑∞​αt​(s,a)2<∞,αt​(s,a)∈[0,1].

Under these conditions, Theorem 6.1 gives Qt​→Q∗ with probability 1.

Note that the first condition already implies that each state-action pair (s,a) must be visited infinitely often. A concrete way to achieve all three conditions is to use an exploration policy that visits every (s,a) infinitely often together with a per-coordinate learning rate αt​(s,a)=1/nt​(s,a), where nt​(s,a) counts the number of visits to (s,a) up to time t. This satisfies ∑αt​(s,a)=∑k=1∞​1/k=∞ and ∑αt​(s,a)2=∑k=1∞​1/k2<∞.

7. Exact policy evaluation

In Exercise 3.4, we showed that iterating Bπ​ converges to Vπ​; this is the numerical policy evaluation scheme used in the ARENA materials. When the state space is finite and the dynamics (T,R) are known, there is also an exact (closed-form) solution: the Bellman equation becomes a linear system that can be solved directly. In this problem we derive that closed form for deterministic policies.

Definition 7.1 (Matrix-vector notation for a deterministic policy). Fix a deterministic policy π. Treating the value function as a vector in R∣S∣, define:

  • vπ∈R∣S∣ with vsπ​:=Vπ​(s),
  • Pπ∈R∣S∣×∣S∣ with Ps,s′π​:=T(s′∣s,π(s)) (the transition matrix under π),
  • Rπ∈R∣S∣×∣S∣ with Rs,s′π​:=R(s,π(s),s′) (the reward matrix),
  • rπ∈R∣S∣ with rsπ​:=∑s′​Ps,s′π​Rs,s′π​=∑s′​T(s′∣s,π(s))R(s,π(s),s′) (the expected immediate reward).

Fact 7.2 (Neumann series). Equip Rn×n with the induced ∞-norm

∥A∥∞​:=imax​j∑​∣Aij​∣(maximum absolute row sum).

If ∥A∥∞​<1, then I−A is invertible, and

(I−A)−1=k=0∑∞​Ak.

Exercise 7.1. Starting from the Bellman equation (Exercise 1.1) applied to a deterministic policy π, show that

Exact Policy Evaluation

vπ=(I−γPπ)−1rπ,

assuming I−γPπ is invertible (which we prove in Exercise 7.2).

Hint: specialize the Bellman equation to a deterministic policy and write the resulting system of ∣S∣ equations in matrix-vector form.

Solution

Since π is deterministic, π(a∣s)=[[a=π(s)]], and the Bellman equation from Exercise 1.1 collapses the sum over actions:

Vπ​(s)=s′∈S∑​T(s′∣s,π(s))(R(s,π(s),s′)+γVπ​(s′)).

Splitting the reward and value terms and rewriting with the matrix notation of Definition 7.1:

vsπ​​=s′∑​Ps,s′π​Rs,s′π​+γs′∑​Ps,s′π​vs′π​=rsπ​+γ(Pπvπ)s​.​

This holds for every s, so in vector form

vπ=rπ+γPπvπ⟺(I−γPπ)vπ=rπ.

Assuming I−γPπ is invertible, left-multiplying by its inverse gives vπ=(I−γPπ)−1rπ.

Exercise 7.2. Prove that I−γPπ is invertible for any deterministic policy π and any γ∈(0,1).

Hint: apply Fact 7.2.

Solution

The matrix Pπ is row-stochastic: Ps,s′π​≥0 and ∑s′​Ps,s′π​=∑s′​T(s′∣s,π(s))=1 for every s. Therefore

∥Pπ∥∞​=smax​s′∑​∣Ps,s′π​∣=smax​s′∑​Ps,s′π​=1,

and so ∥γPπ∥∞​=γ<1. By the Neumann series (Fact 7.2), I−γPπ is invertible, with

(I−γPπ)−1=k=0∑∞​(γPπ)k=k=0∑∞​γk(Pπ)k.

Combining with Exercise 7.1,

vπ=k=0∑∞​γk(Pπ)krπ,

which has a direct interpretation: (Pπ)krπ is the vector of expected rewards exactly k steps into the future under π, and vπ is their discounted sum.

Remark. The same derivation extends to stochastic policies by defining Ps,s′π​=∑a​π(a∣s)T(s′∣s,a) and rsπ​=∑a​π(a∣s)∑s′​T(s′∣s,a)R(s,a,s′). The matrix Pπ remains row-stochastic, so the argument above applies unchanged.

References

M. L. Puterman (1994). Markov Decision Processes --- Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming. Wiley.

John N. Tsitsiklis (1994). Asynchronous Stochastic Approximation and Q-Learning. Machine Learning.

Footnotes

  1. Noting that S×A×S is a finite set, this implies that the rewards are bounded above by Rmax​=maxs,a,s′​R(s,a,s′). ↩
